b.bio: Born at Rushden, Northamptonshire, son of a clergyman; educated at Trinity College, Oxford, where he took his B.A. in 1657, M.A. in 1660, and a fellowship in 1664. Seth Ward, bishop of Salisbury, made him chaplain in 1668 and gave him prebends at Yatesbury and Husborn-Tarrant with Burbage. In 1669 he became perpetual curate of St Thomas's and rector of St Edmund's, Salisbury; in 1672 he was installed precentor there and accumulated B.D. and D.D. He began publishing against Roman Catholic doctrine in 1664, attacking Serenus Cressy, was answered by John Sergeant, whom he replied to in 1666, and continued anti-Romish polemic until 1689. An Arminian within the Church of England, he later showed Unitarian leanings.
b.s: The works held here are chiefly his anti-Catholic polemics — against host-worship, traditions, the fallibility claims of Rome, and the antiquity of Romish doctrine — plus his large paraphrase on the epistles and his reply to Sergeant's Sure Footing.

A sermon preach'd to the Society, for reformation of manners at Kingstone upon Thames, on July 17th 1700. Publish'd at the request of the…
The royal politician represented in one hundred emblems written in Spanish by Don Diego Saavedra Faxardo ... ; with a large preface,…

b.bio: Dominicus à Portonariis is the Latinized name of Domingo de Portonariis de Ursino, a Spanish printer active in Salamanca from 1569 to 1577 and in Zaragoza from 1578 to 1585. His device bore the motto 'In virtute oculi et manus.' He printed legal, theological, and literary works, including Gregorio López's glossed Siete Partidas (1576), Jiménez Arias's Lexicon ecclesiasticum (1572), and romances of chivalry such as Florisel de Niquea and Belianís de Grecia. The piece held here under his name is a printer's preface ('To the reader') to an edition of the medieval Spanish chronicle of Roderick Ximénez, archbishop of Toledo.
b.s: His preface defends editorial method for the chronicle of Roderick Ximénez: corrupt passages are to be marked rather than emended, and he weighs the authorities of Geoffrey the monk, Abbot Alexander, and Trithemius on chronology and on Alberia, daughter of King Alfonso.

w: Annotation on the Doctrine of Cassian

b.bio: Spanish Dominican theologian born at Medina de Rioseco (Medina de Rio-Seco), Old Castile, about 1550. He taught theology for twenty years in Spain (Burgos, Trianos, Plasencia, Valladolid) and for ten years (1596–1606) at the Minerva in Rome, where he arrived on 7 November 1596 and shortly after presented Clement VIII a memorial requesting examination of Molina's Concordia liberi Arbitrii. Before the Congregatio de Auxiliis he defended the Thomist doctrines of grace and predestination alone for three years, then jointly with Thomas de Lemos, until the congregation's suspension in 1606. Paul V appointed him to the archbishopric of Trani on 19 March 1606, where he remained until his death.
b.s: Chief Dominican spokesman against Molinism at the Congregatio de Auxiliis; the annotation held here extends his anti-Molinist case backward onto Cassian and the Semi-Pelagians, arguing that they denied preventing grace.

w: Historical fragment concerning the life of Hatto and Berhard

b.bio: Dado was bishop of Verdun from 880 to 923, in the final decades of the Carolingian empire. Geschichtsquellen also credits him with a Historia sui temporis. The work held here, De Vita Hattonis et Berhardi Praedecessorum Suorum, is a short historical account of his two predecessors as bishops of Verdun. It records how Hatto and Bernhard enriched the church of Verdun through royal and imperial grants — charters cited include those of Emperor Lothair, King Charles, Louis the German, Emperor Charles, King Arnulf, and King Lothair — established canons on endowed properties, and secured abbey grants by royal precept, presenting episcopal endowment as continued by divine disposition.
b.s: His fragment is a contemporary witness to how a Carolingian bishop's see accumulated property through imperial and royal charters, told through the lives of the bishops who did it.

b.bio: Dagobert I, son of Chlothar II, ruled Austrasia from 623 and the whole Frankish realm from 629 until his death on 19 January 639; he has been described as the last Merovingian king to wield real royal power and was the first Frankish king buried at Saint-Denis. The work held here under his name is a set of ecclesiastical precepts: royal charters confirming donations of monasteries to churches, asserting that bishops hold perpetual authority over donated houses, that written charters preserve memory and prevent fraud, and that such grants bind successors irrevocably. It names Archbishop Modoald of Trier and Archbishop Cunibert of Cologne among its figures.
b.s: The precepts show how Merovingian kingship framed pious royal donation as true worship and protection of the church as securing divine favor on the kingdom.

b.bio: Dagobert II was a Merovingian king of Austrasia. Son of Sigebert III, he was exiled after his father's death in 656 and lived as a monk in Ireland; Wilfrid of York helped arrange his return, and he reigned from 675 or 676 until his assassination in 679 near Stenay. His violent death earned him veneration as a martyr in Lorraine from at least the ninth century. The work held here under his name is not a theological treatise but a royal act: grants of imperial baths and estates to Wissembourg abbey, framed as almsgiving for the soul.
b.s: The single work held here shows Merovingian kingship acting through ecclesiastical donation: royal grants to priests and monasteries are presented as remedies for the donor's soul, with royal protection guaranteeing monastic possessions.

b.bio: Dagulf was a scribe at Charlemagne's court who produced the psalter now known by his name between 782 and 795. The manuscript, written entirely in golden Carolingian minuscule and containing the Psalms and Frankish canticles, was intended as a gift from Charlemagne to Pope Hadrian I, apparently to mend relations strained by the Libri Carolini; Hadrian's death in 795 meant it likely never reached Rome.
b.s: The library holds an eighteen-line poem in which Dagulf describes the golden psalter he wrote as a royal gift, presenting the pious king as joining David's choir.

b.bio: Damian was Bishop of Pavia (Ticinum), succeeding Anastasius (elected 680 according to Wikipedia and Catholic Online; c. 685 per the New Catholic Encyclopedia), and acted as mediator between the Lombards and the Byzantine emperors. As a priest he opposed Monothelitism at the Synod of Milan (680) and composed the letter sent in the name of Bishop Mansuetus of Milan to Emperor Constantine IV; this letter, read at the Third Council of Constantinople, professed two natural wills and two natural operations in Christ. It is his only extant writing, though it is sometimes attributed to Mansuetus on whose behalf Damian wrote. Sources give his death variously as 710 or at Pavia on April 4, c. 715.
b.s: The single work held here is his anti-Monothelite epistle to Emperor Constantine IV, a creedal defense of dyothelite Christology read at Constantinople III.

w: Privilege for the Collegiate Church of St. Mary of Huy

b.bio: Theodwin (Dietwinus), printed here as Deoduin, was a Bavarian named by Emperor Henry III to the see of Liège in 1048. He led an imperial victory over Dirk IV of Frisia in 1049 and in 1050–51 wrote to Henry I of France urging action against Berengar of Tours. In 1066 he granted city rights to Huy, the oldest surviving such charter from present-day Belgium, and built, consecrated and endowed its collegiate church of St. Mary with fifteen prebends. On 23 March 1075 Gregory VII reproached him by letter for lax clerical discipline; he died on 23 June 1075 and was buried at Huy.
b.s: The works held here are charters and letters of a prince-bishop: liberties granted to local churches, lay custody of church property during vacancies, secular enforcement of ecclesiastical rights against bishops, charters confirmed by anathema, and a letter against Bruno of Angers and Berengarius of Tours defending the eucharist as Christ's true body.

b.bio: The library prints one work under this name in PL 155: a two-page text called 'Itineraries', exegetical and hortatory in character, citing Augustine. None of the surviving records describes this author. They concern two later Irishmen of similar name: Dermod O'Meara (fl. 1610–1646), physician and poet of Ormonde, author of Ormonius and De Moribus; and Dermot O'Hurley (c. 1530–1584), Archbishop of Cashel, martyred under Elizabeth I and beatified in 1992. Neither was a patristic writer, and neither matches the loci or form of the work held here. Nothing else is asserted about the author.
b.s: The work here treats last things, providence, grace, and prayer, arguing that Babylon signifies the present wicked world, that the devil lays snares for the faithful, that God warns sinners by temporal calamities, and that bodily death is milder than eternal hellfire.

b.bio: Desiderius, called Didier in French sources, was born around 580 at Albi or Obrege to a noble family of Aquitaine. Educated with his brothers Rusticus and Syagrius at the court-school of Chlotar II, he served as royal treasurer, retaining the office under Dagobert, before entering the church. Ordained bishop of Cahors on April 8, 630 by Sulpitius the Pious of Bourges, he succeeded his murdered brother Rusticus and governed the diocese until his death on November 15, 655, a date Krusch has questioned.
b.s: The library holds ten pages of his letters from PL 87, which defend him against accusers including Felix of Narbonne and treat prayer, royal judgment, almsgiving, and eternal reward for benefiting the church.

b.bio: Born Dauferius of a non-regnant branch of the Lombard dukes of Benevento, he entered monastic life under the name Desiderius and joined Monte Cassino in 1055. He was abbot from 1058 to 1087, a period its own writers and Gregory VII described as the monastery's golden age of political, intellectual and artistic influence; its monks filled south Italian bishoprics and included cardinals. Created cardinal by Nicholas II on 6 March 1058, he was elected pope on 24 May 1086 as Victor III, succeeding Gregory VII, was consecrated on 9 May 1087, and died on 16 September 1087.
b.s: The works here are his Dialogues — defending miracles worked through saints and the edifying force of virtuous examples — and an epitaph for Apollinaris, both written as abbot of Monte Cassino.

w: Fragments of the book on the privileges and authority of the Roman Church
Preface to the collection of canons

b.bio: Born at Todi, Deusdedit entered the Benedictine Order and was raised to the cardinalate by Gregory VII with the title of San Pietro in Vincoli. He took part in the Roman synod of 1078 and served as one of Gregory VII's chief agents in the conflict against imperial control of the Church. At Gregory's prompting he compiled a collection of canons, completed in 1087 and dedicated to Victor III. The fragments held here defend papal authority against Henry IV and the antipope Guibert of Ravenna.
b.s: His works here are Gregorian polemic: fragments arguing that no one may judge or depose a pope, that Henry IV tyrannically installed the simoniac antipope Guibert, and that the emperor's broken oath at Canossa justified excommunication.

w: Letter on the Calculation of Easter
Letters on the calculation of Easter

b.bio: Dionysius Exiguus ('the Humble') was a monk born in Scythia Minor (modern Romania) who lived in Rome from around 500 until his death before 544. Cassiodorus calls him a Scythian, learned in both Greek and Latin; later writers honor him as an abbot, though Cassiodorus describes him as still an ordinary monk late in life. He translated 401 church canons from Greek into Latin — the Apostolic Canons, Nicaea, Constantinople, Chalcedon, Sardica — and compiled the decretals of popes from Siricius to Anastasius II. His Collectiones canonum Dionysianae carried great authority in the West. At Pope John I's request he prepared in 525 the Easter reckoning that introduced Anno Domini dating. The works here include his canonical collections and Easter letters alongside his Latin translations: Gregory of Nyssa on the creation of man, the Life of Pachomius, and the finding of John the Baptist's head. A Synodal Letter is also held under his name, though some works long attributed to him (e.g. Cyril of Alexandria's synodical letter) are now assigned to Marius Mercator.
b.s: The works held here are the foundations of Western canon law and the Easter computus that gave the Christian calendar its AD numbering.

b.bio: Furius Dionysius Filocalus was a Roman scribe and stone engraver, specialist in epigraphic texts, active in the second half of the fourth century. He served as the official engraver of Pope Damasus and described himself as 'Damasi pappae cultor atque amator' — admirer and friend of the pope. His best-known work is the Chronography of 354 (Calendar of 354), commissioned by a wealthy Roman Christian named Valentinus; the original is lost, known through later copies including a seventeenth-century Barberini manuscript reproducing a lost Carolingian Codex Luxemburgensis. The library holds a five-page calendar text under his name in PL 13.
b.s: His Calendar of 354 is the oldest known Christian calendar and contains the first known reference to the celebration of Christmas, alongside Roman festivities.

b.bio: A collective designation, not an individual: the library holds under this name a two-page 'Censure' printed in PL 178, a polemical survey of condemned positions attributed to the doctors of the Paris schools. The text argues against Abelard on seventeen points and once against Norbert, treating baptism, Christ, faith, grace, justification, last things, sin, predestination, sacraments, and the church. Among its theses: the devil acquired no right over fallen man; Mary was sanctified without contracting original sin; the Word assumed human nature; infants lack elicited acts of charity. It cites Abelard most, then Bernard. None of The surviving records describes this corporate author; they concern John of Paris, Peter Lombard, and Nicholas of Lyra — different persons — and are set aside as homonym or context material.
b.s: The work here is a concise record of what the Paris masters censured in Abelard's theology, useful as a snapshot of mid-twelfth-century doctrinal controversy.

b.bio: Dhuoda, whom the library prints under the Latinized forms Dodana sive Duodena, was a Frankish noblewoman who married Bernard, Duke of Septimania and Count of Barcelona, at Aachen in 824 (the exact day is contested). Her only biographical source is the Liber Manualis itself. Separated from her husband and both sons — William a hostage at the court of Charles the Bald, the infant Bernard taken to Aquitaine — she wrote the Manual for William's education, beginning it 30 November 841 at Uzès and completing it 2 February 843. She describes herself as weak and near death; she probably did not live long after finishing it.
b.s: The Liber Manualis is a rare surviving work of moral and religious instruction by a Carolingian woman, teaching prayer (uniting mouth, heart, and works), love of God, baptism, and hope of eternal life.

b.bio: None of the supplied biographical sources describes this author; they concern other figures (Dominic of Evesham, an early-twelfth-century prior and hagiographer of Evesham Abbey, and Chromatius, late-fourth-century bishop of Aquileia) and must not be used for him. The name as printed belongs to a Latin churchman associated with the see of Grado/Aquileia. The library holds one page under his name: a letter to Peter of Antioch.
b.s: His single held work is a Latin polemical letter to Peter of Antioch defending the rank of Grado against the Constantinopolitan clergy, asserting Peter's primacy of honor among churches, apostolic founding as the basis of patriarchal status, and the necessity of participation in Christ's body in the Eucharist for eternal life.

w: Excerpts from the Life of Matilda
On the Life of Duchess Matilda

b.bio: Donizo (also Domnizo, Donizone) of Canossa was an Italian Benedictine monk, born c. 1071/2 perhaps at Canossa or Parma. He entered the monastery of Sant'Apollonio at Canossa c. 1086/7 and was its abbot by 1136. His chief work is the Vita Mathildis, a life of Matilda of Tuscany in leonine hexameters, written between 1111 and 1115 and hastily re-dedicated to Empress Matilda after the countess died in July 1115. Book one treats the princes of Canossa and their castle; book two treats Matilda herself. He also left a fragmentary verse commentary on Genesis, the Enarratio Genesis.
b.s: The Vita Mathildis is a principal contemporary source for Matilda of Tuscany, her dynasty, and the Gregorian Reform and Investiture Controversy; the library holds it with later excerpted lives of Matilda, which present saintly rulers as exemplars of love of God and church, with loyalty to the see of Peter as marking true Catholic princes.

b.bio: Domnolus was first abbot of Saint-Laurent in Paris. He declined the bishopric of Avignon offered by King Clotaire I, and in 559 became bishop of Le Mans, serving until his death on December 1, 581. He attended the Synod of Tours (567 by one source; 566 by another) and built churches, monasteries, and a hospice for pilgrims on the Sarthe. Gregory of Tours records miracles worked at his hands (Historia Francorum 6.9; 9.39). The library holds under his name only a two-page Testament from PL 72.
b.s: The work held here is his Testament, which asserts that the church holds donated goods not by hereditary right and that violating ecclesiastical donation incurs divine curse — an early witness to Merovingian thinking on church property.

b.bio: A French prelate made bishop of Beauvais in 1030; in 1035 he founded the convent of St. Symphorien-les-Beauvais. King Henry I's diplomas describe him as wholly given over to divine religion ('vir divinae religioni totus mancipatus'). He died at Beauvais on April 21, 1047. He is not the Carolingian Drogo of Metz nor the anchorite Drogo of Sebourg.
b.s: The library holds his single-page letter to a fellow bishop arguing that violence against clergy is sacrilege against God's temple, that Christ identifies himself with his ministers, that sacrilege against clergy admits no delay of penalty, that excommunication declares divine judgment already passed, and that triple restitution with penance suffices — citing capitularies, the Salic law, and Louis father of Lothair against those who despise unworthy priests.

w: Monastic Agreement of the English Nation

b.bio: Dunstan was an English Benedictine monk who served successively as Abbot of Glastonbury Abbey, Bishop of Worcester, Bishop of London, and Archbishop of Canterbury, and acted as an important minister of state to several English kings. His birth year is disputed: the Catholic Encyclopedia notes that Osbern's date of 924/5 has been rejected by some scholars, while Wikipedia gives c. 909; both agree he died 19 May 988 at Canterbury. His work restored monastic life in England and reformed the English Church.
b.s: The works here concern the uniformity of monastic custom under one rule and royal authority in reforming the church's worship — the program with which Dunstan's name is associated in the English monastic reform.

b.bio: The library prints this name as 'Durand of Auvergne' and holds one work under it: an Epistle to Anselm printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina vol. 150. That volume belongs to eleventh-century material, so the author here cannot be the better-known Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1332/1334), the Dominican bishop of Meaux whose dates fall two centuries later and whose works are Sentences commentaries, not letters to Anselm. the surviving records describe only that later namesake; they say nothing about the author of this epistle.
b.s: The single held work is a letter addressed to Anselm, preserved in PL 150; nothing further about its argument or authorship is established by the record or the sources given.

b.bio: Dynamius the Patrician was an aristocrat of Massalia (Marseille) in Gallia Narbonensis who died in 601. He wrote in south-east Gaul around 580/590, when he composed the Life of Maximus, bishop of Riez, at the request of Urbicus, the current bishop of Riez. The library holds under his name the Life of St. Maximus, the Life of St. Marius (abbot of the monastery of Bodonensis), and two letters. Some manuscripts attribute the Marius vita to a 'Dinamius presbyter', and some catalogues list variant identifications ('Dynamius Lerinensis', 'Pseudo-Dynamius'); the works held here are those printed under Dynamius Patricius in PL 80.
b.s: His Lives of Maximus of Riez and Marius are early Merovingian saints' lives that present ascetic renunciation as bloodless martyrdom and the saint's merits as lasting protection for his city.

b.bio: Leander was born at Carthage around 534 to a Roman family that moved to Seville about 554. After life as a monk, he became Bishop of Seville in 579, the leading Catholic see under the Arian Visigothic kings. He was instrumental in the conversions of Prince Hermenegild and King Reccared to Catholicism, and played a leading part in the events culminating in the conversion council of 589. His siblings included Isidore, his successor as bishop of Seville, Fulgentius, bishop of Carthagena, and Florentina, a nun. He died at Seville on 13 March 600 or 601.
b.s: The work held here is his preface in PL 18 (10 pp.). Leander matters chiefly as the bishop who led the Visigoths' conversion to Catholicism; his wider corpus includes the rule for nuns addressed to his sister Florentina.

b.bio: Dominicus Mita is known to the sources as the editor of the 1750 Venetian edition of Peter Chrysologus's Sermones, described as the most corrected and augmented edition, with sermons added from St. Augustine and from Luca d'Acheriis. The edition includes editorial notes drawing on collations of manuscripts, selected observations of Mita himself, variant readings of Latino Latini, and corrections of Meursius. The works held here under his name — a life of Peter Chrysologus, testimonies, a preface, and a response to opposing arguments — are the editorial apparatus of that edition: a biography asserting Chrysologus was consecrated bishop in 433 and died in 450, and polemic against Eutyches, Nestorius, and Arianism. A canonist named Dominicus de Sancto Geminiano (died and buried in Bologna; professor at Bologna, Auditor Camerae at Rome) appears in some literature but is a different person.
b.s: His 1750 Venetian edition presented itself as the most corrected and augmented edition of Chrysologus's Sermones, with manuscript collations and editorial notes; the Migne volume held here contains his editorial apparatus.

b.bio: Daniel Papebrochius (Papebroch), born in Antwerp on 17 March 1628, entered the Society of Jesus and was ordained a priest in 1658. From 1659 he worked under Jean Bolland on the Acta Sanctorum, traveling to Italian archives in 1660–1662 and later editing volumes for March, April, May, and part of June. His historical criticism of monastic charters led him to doubt the Carmelite claim of descent from Elijah, provoking attacks from that order; Spanish Inquisition tribunals at Toledo condemned fourteen volumes of the Acta in 1695 and 1697, though Rome condemned only a papal chronology.
b.s: The work held here is his preliminary commentary to the Acta Sanctorum volume for St. Norbert, defending the founder of the Premonstratensians against critics such as Michael Malcorpius and Joannes Le Paige and arguing that immemorial cult suffices for declaring universal sanctity.

b.bio: No surviving record identifies a writer named Dionysius Ramazini. The three biographical sources retrieved describe different men entirely: Denis the Carthusian (1402–1471), a Carthusian monk of Roermond; Dionysius Exiguus (c. 470–c. 544), the Scythian-born monk in Rome known for his Easter computus and canon collections; and Denis Lambin (1520–1572), a French classical scholar. None matches the name as printed, and none can be credited with the work held here. What can be said comes from the library record alone: one page, a dedication letter printed in PL 61, framed as history and naming Paulinus alongside popes Gregory XII, Eugenius IV, and Paul II — popes of the fifteenth century, which would place the text well after the patristic era.
b.s: The library holds only a single-page dedication letter (PL 61); its citation of fifteenth-century popes suggests a late medieval text shelved among the Latin Fathers rather than a patristic work.

b.bio: Domenico Riviera was born at Urbino on 3 December 1671 and studied at Bologna before taking degrees in both laws (utroque iure) at Urbino. Trained as coadjutor under the erudite Raffaello Fabretti, he succeeded him as archivist of Castel Sant'Angelo in 1700, an office that grounded his antiquarian and documentary method. He undertook a diplomatic mission in 1707 (to Prince Eugene of Savoy), was created cardinal on 2 March 1733, became Cardinal-Priest of Santi Quirico e Giulitta and then of Santi XII Apostoli, took part in the conclave of 1740, and died on 2 November 1752.
b.s: The library holds his Life of Jerome (PL 22), a historical and polemical study that fixes Jerome's birth in 346 and his baptism as an adult, locates Stridon in Istria near Aquileia, and weighs Jerome's quarrels with Rufinus, John of Jerusalem, Jovinian, the Origenists and the Pelagians from the sources.

b.bio: Denis de Sainte-Marthe, born in Paris on 24 May 1650 and died there on 30 March 1725, was a Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, theologian and historian, who served as the congregation's superior general from 1720 to 1725. Educated at the Maurist college of Pontlevoy, he entered the abbey of Saint-Melaine in Rennes as a novice in 1668 and later taught philosophy and theology at Saint-Rémi in Reims, Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and Saint-Denis. He wrote against Calvinist and Protestant theses, produced a history of St. Gregory the Great, and worked on the Gallia Christiana, the great survey of French ecclesiastical provinces begun by members of his own family.
b.s: The works held here are his prefatory historical notices to volumes of Migne's Patrologia Latina, where he introduces patristic authors such as Leo the Great and Martial of Limoges, defends Martial as an apostle against those who ranked him only among the confessors, and treats church history and true worship against Manichaean-offshoot heretics.

b.bio: Domenico Vallarsi, born and died in Verona (13 November 1702 – 14 August 1771), was an Italian priest trained with the Jesuits who devoted himself to archaeological and patristic scholarship. The city of Verona, its bishop, and Benedict XIV — who gave him a benefice in the Diocese of Vicenza and named him reviser at the Holy Office for the Oriental languages — supported his manuscript searches. He corresponded with Muratori, Zeno, and Mazzucchelli. His chief work is an eleven-volume edition of Jerome's complete works (Verona 1734–42; enlarged Venice 1766–72), reproduced in the Patrologia Latina (the library holds its first volume, PL 22); he also assisted Scipio Maffei on Hilary and began an edition of Rufinus (1745).
b.s: The works held here are his prefatory matter to volume one of that Jerome edition: a dedication to Clement XII, general prefaces, and a proposed new chronological ordering of Jerome's epistles, defending Jerome against Origenists and against earlier editors from Erasmus and Martianay to the Benedictine/Maurist editors.

b.bio: Demetrios Kydones, born in Thessalonica in 1324 and died on Crete in 1398 (one reference gives 1397), was a Byzantine theologian, translator, and statesman who served three terms as Mesazon under John VI Kantakouzenos, John V Palaiologos, and Manuel II Palaiologos. A student of Nilos Kabasilas, he went to Italy in 1354, embraced Latin Scholasticism, translated Augustine and Aquinas into Greek, and made a profession of the Latin faith by 1365. His policy sought union with Rome to secure Western military aid against the Ottomans. His brother Prochoros was a noted anti-Palamite. Note: the PG 154 volume held here also contains works by other authors printed alongside his orations.
b.s: His own works in this volume are chiefly anti-Islamic polemics and deliberative orations—arguments that the Alcoran is not the law of God and appeals against surrendering Gallipoli—written in service of his Latin-union, anti-Ottoman program. However, much of the volume's 630 pages consists of works by other authors (e.g., John Cantacuzenus's apologies, a translation of Brother Richard's treatise), so the volume as a whole cannot be described as wholly his.
